bib.title: GraphReader: Building Graph-based Agent to Enhance Long-Context Abilities of Large Language Models

legacy_report:
SOURCE: GraphReader: Building Graph-based Agent to Enhance Long-Context Abilities of Large Language Models. Shilong Li*, Yancheng He*, Hangyu Guo*, Xingyuan Bu*†‡ (corresponding author), Ge Bai, Jie Liu, Jiaheng Liu, Xingwei Qu, Yangguang Li, Wanli Ouyang, Wenbo Su, Bo Zheng. Affiliations: Alibaba Group, CUHK, Shanghai AI Lab, Univ. Manchester. The PDF header reads "arXiv:2406.14550v2 [cs.CL] 5 Nov 2024". No venue is printed in the text, so treat it as an arXiv preprint (2024, v2).

COVERAGE: 83,239 of 83,239 chars read (main text, limitations, tables 1-9, appendices A-I including the prompts and the example case). The references were skimmed. The figure images (the plot data in Figs 1, 3, 4, 5) were not rendered, so I could not read exact curve values from them.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: With a 4k window, GraphReader beats GPT-4-128k full-text reading on HotpotWikiQA-mixup at every length from 16k to 256k. The gap widens as context grows.
  number: LR-1 at 16k is 42.0 vs 38.0. At 128k it is 28.0 vs 16.0. At 256k it is 30.0 vs 14.0.
  setup: LV-Eval HotpotWikiQA-mixup, 250 samples, avg 142.4k tokens. GPT-4 (gpt-4-1106-preview), temperature 0.2. GraphReader uses a 4k window, 2k chunks, 5 initial nodes, and at most 10 function calls per path. The 128k and 256k inputs are truncated for GPT-4-128k.
  quote: "our method achieves a performance gain of 10.53% relatively on LR-1 over GPT-4-128k full-text reading under 16k context length. With the context length increasing to 128k, our method achieves a performance gain of 75.00% relatively over GPT-4-128k."
  where: Sec 4.2 and Table 3, p.6-7

- claim: Plain RAG (BM25 or Ada-002 embeddings) is the weakest method. The authors say retrieval fails to recall all the chunks that hold the supporting facts.
  number: On HotpotQA, BM25 top-1 gets LR-1 57.7 and Ada-002 top-3 gets 72.0, against 84.3 for GraphReader. On MuSiQue, BM25 top-1 gets 33.0 against 59.0.
  setup: LongBench subsets, 4k window, GPT-4 reader. The tables give no per-chunk token size for the RAG baselines beyond "4k".
  quote: "A possible reason is that text retrieval has difficulty recalling all chunks that contain the supporting facts for answering the input question."
  where: Sec 4.2 Results of RAG methods, Table 2

- claim: On the four LongBench QA sets (3 multi-hop, 1 single-hop), GraphReader at 4k is best on all four metrics except a few ties. It beats GPT-4-128k full read, ReadAgent, PEARL, LongRAG and GraphRAG, and comes close to the "Golden" setting where the supporting facts are given directly.
  number: HotpotQA LR-1 84.3 / F1 70.0 (GPT-4-128k 83.3 / 68.4, Golden 92.3 / 73.8). 2Wiki LR-1 83.7 (ReadAgent 79.0, GraphRAG 67.7). MuSiQue LR-1 59.0 (ReadAgent 54.5, GraphRAG 46.5). NarrativeQA LR-1 65.0, F1 29.8 (GPT-4-128k 63.5, 29.4).
  setup: Datasets of 200-300 samples, avg 8.8k-29.7k tokens, so they fit in a 128k window. The authors note that this reduces "lost in the middle" for the full-read baseline. Margins over full read on HotpotQA and NarrativeQA are small (about 1 to 1.5 points), and there are no variance figures or seeds.
  quote: "GraphReader | 4k | 84.3 89.7 55.0 70.0 83.7 87.0 59.3 70.1 59.0 63.5 38.0 47.4 65.0 80.0 15.5 29.8"
  where: Table 2, p.5

- claim: Choosing nodes by reasoning matters more than the rational plan. Random initial and neighbor node selection costs about 18% on average. Removing the rational plan costs a few points.
  number: HotpotQA LR-1 is 84.3 full, 81.7 without plan, 66.0 with random node selection. MuSiQue is 59.0, 56.0 and 35.0. NarrativeQA LR-1 is 65.0, 63.0 and 53.0.
  setup: Ablation on the four LongBench sets, GPT-4 agent.
  quote: "random selection results in a significant performance drop, with an average decline of 18%."
  where: Sec 4.3, Table 4

- claim: GraphReader's token cost per question is only slightly above ReadAgent's. The graph is built once per document, so many questions on one document amortise the cost.
  number: 52.8k vs 48.7k tokens per question, a ratio of 1.08.
  setup: HotpotWikiQA-mixup-256k, avg context 358.3k tokens. Cost counts input and output tokens during exploration only. Graph-construction tokens are not shown in Table 5 (my reading of the table). The text says only that one graph is built per document.
  quote: "GraphReader uses only 1.08 times more tokens than ReadAgent (52.8k / 48.7k), yet achieves more than double the performance improvement"
  where: Sec 4.4 Cost Analysis, Table 5

- claim: GraphReader keeps about 60% supporting-fact recall at 256k, while the baselines decline sharply. Notes in the notebook recover more supporting facts than the atomic facts alone.
  number: Table 6 on HotpotQA. SF-wise recall is 76.4% for atomic facts and 90.5% for the final notebook. Sample-wise recall is 64.7% and 85.3%.
  setup: Recall is judged by GPT-4-128k at temperature 0.1 on HotpotWikiQA-mixup (Fig 5) and HotpotQA (Table 6). The 60% figure is read from the text, because the Fig 5 curves were not extracted.
  quote: "GraphReader maintains around 60% recall at 256k context length, in contrast to the significant degradation in ReadAgent."
  where: Sec 4.4, Fig 5, Table 6

- claim: Two hyperparameters have interior optima. Best performance is at 5 initial nodes and a 2k chunk size.
  number: 5 initial nodes; L = 2k, tested at 1k/2k/4k/6k.
  setup: Node counts 1/3/5/7 on 2Wiki and NarrativeQA (Fig 3). Chunk size tested on 256k HotpotWikiQA-mixup (Fig 4).
  quote: "Increasing the number of nodes improves performance up to a certain point, with optimal performance at 5 initial nodes"
  where: Sec 4.3, Figs 3-4

- claim: Extra real-world benchmarks: GraphReader leads on QuALITY and Natural Questions too.
  number: QuALITY LR-1 57.3 vs GPT-4-128k 45.7. Natural Questions LR-1 79.0 vs 75.0 (LongRAG 77.7).
  setup: Table 7, 4k window vs 128k baselines. The sample count is not given in the text I read.
  quote: "GraphReader | 4k | 57.3 82.3 4.3 14.3 79.0 84.7 48.3 62.1"
  where: Appendix E, Table 7

- claim: The agent is efficient. It averages 3 to 4 function calls per question. Multi-hop QA uses read_neighbor_node most, and single-hop QA uses read_chunk most.
  number: Avg calls are HotpotQA 3.0, 2Wiki 3.2, MuSiQue 3.5, NarrativeQA 3.9.
  setup: Table 8 (its caption says MuSiQue and NarrativeQA, but it lists four datasets).
  quote: "each piece of data will perform an average of 3 to 4 actions"
  where: Appendix G

- claim: The graph is large and dense. Nodes grow with text length, with about 10 neighbours per node and about 2 atomic facts per node.
  number: At 256k there are an average of 14,853 nodes and 8,633 atomic facts per graph, with 12.2 neighbours per node. At 16k there are 1,741.6 nodes and 749.7 atomic facts.
  setup: Table 9. Extraction is done by GPT-4 per 2k chunk, with extraction output capped at 1024 tokens.
  quote: "After normalization, each node has an average of about 10 neighbor nodes."
  where: Appendix H, Table 9

MECHANISM (for the note)
- Construction: split into chunks of at most L (2k) tokens, keeping paragraph structure. The LLM extracts atomic facts plus key elements per chunk. Key elements are normalized (Lu et al. 2023). Each node is (key element, its atomic facts). Nodes are linked if one's key element appears in the other's atomic facts.
- Exploration: the agent writes a rational plan, picks N=5 initial nodes, and keeps a notebook. At each node it reads atomic facts, then picks read_chunk(IDs) or stop_and_read_neighbor. It then reads chunks (search_more, read_previous_chunk, read_subsequent_chunk, termination) and then neighbors (read_neighbor_node or termination).
- Answer: notes from the N agents are compiled, then chain-of-thought plus majority voting resolves inconsistencies.
- Quote: "the agent employs a coarse-to-fine strategy, progressing from reading atomic facts to the original text, as all atomic facts can fit within the context window."

LIMITS
- Authors concede two limits. (1) It relies on closed-source GPT-4, so there are QPS and regional limits. (2) Agent efficiency depends on the model's planning and reasoning ability. They name future work on open-source trained models.
- Everything uses GPT-4 (gpt-4-1106-preview) for the graph, the agent and the judge. LLM-rated metrics (LR-1/LR-2) use GPT-4 as rater, so the judge and system share a model family.
- There are no confidence intervals, seeds or significance tests. Several margins are small (HotpotQA, NarrativeQA vs full read). Sample sizes are 200-300 per set, and LV-Eval has 250 at each length, with 50 or fewer per length cell by implication, so one sample is about 2 points. This is my inference from the tables, not a quote.
- The graph-building cost (one LLM call per 2k chunk, over the whole document) is not included in the Table 5 per-question cost. Latency is not reported.
- Benchmarks are Wikipedia QA (plus NarrativeQA and QuALITY), mostly short of 128k. There is no test on code, enterprise documents or dynamic corpora. Results are from 2024 GPT-4, so the long-context baseline has dated, since 128k+ models have improved.
- The GPT-4-128k baseline is truncated at 128k and 256k, which exaggerates the gap at those lengths. The authors note the truncation in the Table 3 caption.
- The baselines GraphRAG and LongRAG are run only on Tables 2 and 7, not on the LV-Eval lengths in Table 3.

BUILDS ON (as printed): ReadAgent (Lee et al., 2024) for gist memory and the LR-1/LR-2 raters. MemWalker (Chen et al., 2023a) and PEARL (Sarthi et al., 2024, as printed) for tree-organised documents. WebGPT (Nakano et al., 2021). KGP (Wang et al., 2024) for graphs of documents. GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024) and LongRAG (Jiang et al., 2024) as baselines. Normalization of key elements (Lu et al., 2023). Chain-of-Thought (Wei et al., 2022). "Lost in the middle" (Liu et al., 2024b). LV-Eval (Yuan et al., 2024) and LongBench (Bai et al., 2023) for benchmarks. Agent planning and reflection (Yao et al., 2022, ReAct-style).

CODE: no code. Prompts are in the appendix: Fig 6 (key element and atomic fact extraction), Fig 7 (rational plan), and Figs 8-12 (node selection, atomic facts, chunks, neighbors, answer). Useful verbatim text: "Atomic Facts: The smallest, indivisible facts, presented as concise sentences." (Fig 6). The Fig 7 example is "Who had a longer tennis career, Danny or Alice?".

FIGURES (captions only, as extracted)
- Fig 1 (p.1): Performance on LV-Eval at 5 context length levels, GraphReader vs ReadAgent, GPT-4-128k, BM25 and Ada-002. It is the quickest view of the scaling gap.
- Fig 2 (p.3): GraphReader pipeline: graph construction, exploration (initial node, atomic facts, chunk queue, neighbors) and answer reasoning. Best single explainer of the mechanism, with a worked Danko Jones / Casa Loma example.
- Fig 3 and Fig 4: initial node count and chunk size sensitivity.
- Fig 5: supporting-fact recall by input length.
- Figs 20-24: worked example. Pairs with the Appendix I walkthrough.

PROBLEMS: Text extraction was clean, except that Fig 2 text is jumbled (diagram labels) and the table columns are flattened (I read the numbers off the row text). No embedded instructions. The target note 04-retrieval.md has no existing mention of GraphReader or li-2024 (grep returned nothing), so this would be a new citation. Venue not printed in the PDF; I did not fill it in from memory. The Table 8 caption mismatches its content (it lists four datasets). One metric is mislabeled in the text ("LLM-Rating-1 (LR-2)").
